content: If isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis (Hr-TB) is suspected, a treatment regimen including isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin (HREZ-levofloxacin) may be initiated while awaiting laboratory confirmation of isoniazid resistance, provided rifampicin resistance has been reliably excluded. For patients already on a standard 2-month HREZ/4-month HR regimen who are later found to have Hr-TB, the HREZ drugs should be continued (or pyrazinamide and ethambutol reintroduced), and levofloxacin added, again ensuring rifampicin resistance is excluded. The duration of the HREZ-levofloxacin regimen is typically determined by the need to complete six months of levofloxacin-containing therapy. In cases where Hr-TB is diagnosed after first-line treatment has started, the patient may end up receiving more than six months of HREZ by the end of treatment. For patients five months into treatment, during the continuation phase, clinicians must assess the patient’s condition to decide whether a six-month course of HREZ-levofloxacin should be initiated at that point. Levofloxacin is recommended for all Hr-TB patients except in specific situations, such as when rifampicin resistance cannot be excluded, there is known or suspected levofloxacin resistance, fluoroquinolone intolerance, a risk of prolonged QT interval, or during pregnancy or breastfeeding (though the latter is not an absolute contraindication). If a fluoroquinolone cannot be used, a six-month HREZ regimen may still be effective. When additional resistance, particularly to pyrazinamide, is suspected or confirmed, individualized treatment regimens must be designed. Testing for isoniazid resistance should ideally include information on specific mutations (katG or inhA), as these may influence treatment design. Increased metabolism of isoniazid due to mutations in the NAT2 gene can reduce its efficacy and increase toxicity in certain individuals. Knowledge of host acetylator status at a regional level may help guide regimen design. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using automated, cartridge-based, and high-throughput diagnostic platforms to detect TB and resistance to rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, and isoniazid. These platforms are an alternative to line probe assays (LPAs) and are widely available in many countries. For children, while only 2% of Hr-TB patients in the reviewed data were pediatric cases, the recommendations for adults can generally be applied to children, as the regimen components are standard pediatric TB medicines. For patients with extensive disease, treatment duration may be extended beyond six months on an individual basis. Among people living with HIV (PLHIV), the priority is to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) within eight weeks of starting TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count. The six-month HREZ-levofloxacin regimen is recommended for PLHIV, as no significant benefit has been observed from extending rifampicin-containing regimens beyond six months in drug-susceptible TB patients on ART. For patients with extrapulmonary Hr-TB, the proposed regimen is likely effective, though no specific data were available. Individualized treatment duration and supportive care may be necessary, particularly for complex cases. Implementation of the HREZ-levofloxacin regimen requires confirmed isoniazid resistance and exclusion of rifampicin resistance. Testing for fluoroquinolone and pyrazinamide resistance is also recommended before starting treatment. If isoniazid susceptibility is later confirmed, levofloxacin can be stopped, and the patient can continue the standard 2HREZ/4HR regimen. Levofloxacin is the preferred fluoroquinolone for Hr-TB treatment due to its well-characterized safety profile, fewer drug interactions compared to moxifloxacin, and its frequent use in studies reviewed for these guidelines. Unlike moxifloxacin, levofloxacin’s pharmacokinetics are not significantly affected by rifampicin. However, levofloxacin may interfere with lamivudine clearance, increasing lamivudine levels, but no dose adjustments are needed. Antacids should be avoided as they impair levofloxacin absorption, but milk products do not require restriction. Treatment beyond six months may be considered for patients with extensive disease or those slow to convert to smear or culture negativity. In such cases, additional resistance to rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, and pyrazinamide must be ruled out. Close monitoring is essential, particularly for liver function due to the hepatotoxic potential of prolonged pyrazinamide use. Monthly testing for AST (SGOT) levels is advised, especially in patients with viral hepatitis or a history of heavy alcohol use. Monitoring for ethambutol toxicity, such as retrobulbar neuritis, is also necessary, particularly in pediatric populations. For multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) patients on longer regimens, monthly sputum culture testing is recommended in addition to smear microscopy to monitor treatment response. Culture testing is more sensitive than microscopy for detecting viable TB bacilli and facilitates phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST). Monthly culture testing increases the detection of true positive results and reduces false negatives compared to smear microscopy alone. However, culture testing requires significant laboratory resources and has a longer turnaround time. Despite these challenges, culture remains a critical tool for monitoring bacteriological status during treatment.
